title: Catch the Milky Way's Dazzling Core at Its Peak This May
summary: If you've ever wanted to witness the Milky Way in all its glory, mark your calendar for mid-May. The moonless nights around the new moon create ideal conditions to spot the glowing band of our galaxy's core, which reaches its highest point in the spring sky between midnight and dawn. During this period, Earth's orbit brings the bright heart of the Milky Way into view—a season astronomers call 'Core Season,' which runs from February to October in the northern hemisphere. But May offers a special advantage over June. The June new moon occurs close to the summer solstice, when twilight lingers longer and eats into the precious dark hours. In May, the window of true darkness is wider, giving you more time to soak in the view. To see it, you'll need to escape city lights. Use a resource like DarkSky.org to find a certified dark sky location near you. Then, direct your gaze to the southern sky. There, you'll see the dense core of our galaxy arching past the constellations Aquila, Scutum, Sagittarius, and Scorpius as it tumbles toward the horizon. What you're actually seeing is a ribbon of interstellar dust, gas, and countless stars—so many that they blend into a soft, glowing band. Smartphone apps like Stellarium or Sky Safari 7 Pro can help you plan your outing by showing exactly where the Milky Way will be at any time. For photographers, this is a dream target. A camera with good low-light performance, like the Nikon Z8 with its full-frame sensor, can capture stunning detail. But even without gear, the naked-eye view is unforgettable. Let your eyes adjust to the dark for at least 20 minutes, and avoid looking at your phone. The Milky Way's core will appear as a hazy, elongated cloud—but knowing it's made of billions of suns makes it one of the most humbling sights in nature. So grab a jacket, find a dark spot, and look up. The galaxy is waiting.
why_it_matters: Recognizing that our Solar System is just a tiny part of a vast galaxy can expand your perspective. Stargazing also raises awareness of light pollution, an environmental issue that affects wildlife and our connection to the night sky.

background_read: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a barred spiral containing hundreds of billions of stars. From Earth, we see its disk edge-on as a faint, glowing band stretching across the sky.

The galaxy's core lies in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, where thick clouds of interstellar dust and a supermassive black hole are hidden. Its visibility from the northern hemisphere is best during spring and summer, when it rises high above the southern horizon.

Light pollution from cities washes out all but the brightest stars for most people. Organizations like the International Dark-Sky Association, which runs DarkSky.org, work to preserve natural night skies.
The new moon phase (when the moon is absent) provides the darkest nights, and in May the combination of a new moon and shorter summer twilight creates a longer window of true darkness than in June.
Digital cameras with full-frame sensors, such as the Nikon Z8, have made astrophotography more accessible, but even the naked-eye view after proper dark adaptation can be life-changing.

perspectives.description: Core Season gives photographers and amateur astronomers a predictable window to capture stunning images and experience the awe of seeing our galaxy's heart. It's a chance to share the beauty with others.

For people living in brightly lit cities, escaping to a dark sky location can be difficult. The Milky Way is invisible to most of the world's population, which many see as a loss of a shared human heritage.

The visibility of the galactic core is a purely astronomical phenomenon tied to Earth's orbit and tilt. This predictable cycle reminds us that our view of the universe is constantly shifting, without deeper meaning.

As LED lighting becomes cheaper and more widespread, light pollution is growing. Balancing safety and visibility with preserving dark skies is a challenge, and this seasonal peak could motivate action to protect night environments.
